Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

point noun

what matters in what is said

also the point, get to the point!, beside the point, get the point?, that’s the main point, up to this point, what’s the point of that?, what’s your point?, you miss the point, but to return to the point, on that point, at this point, the point is, now here’s the point

classical

Ter. Ad. 2.1.31: mitte ista, atque ad rem redī (Lewis & Short s.v. redeō)
Cic. Caecin. 58: nihil ad rem pertinet (Lewis & Short s.v. ad)
Traupman 105: beside the point; get to the point!; get the point?, nihil ad rem; venī ad rem!; tenēsne rem?

rēs, reī f.

noun, fifth declension: ad rem, to the point; nihil ad rem, beside the point

the matter in hand, the point

English “the point” is Latin rēs, the matter itself: ad rem redī, get back to the point; nihil ad rem, nothing to do with the matter; tenēsne rem?, do you follow?

Other words

  • caput, capitis n. — the main point

    in id caput est, quod caput est: that is the main point, the main thing is · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 1.17.4: id quod caput est; Traupman 105: that’s the main point, id caput est; Traupman 106: the point is that I no longer care about such things, quod caput est, jam ista nōn cūrō

    See main.

  • prōpositum, prōpositī n. — the subject in hand: back to the point

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Div. 2.79: sed lābor longius; ad prōpositum revertor (Lewis & Short s.v. lābor); Traupman 105: but to return to the point …, sed ad prōpositum …

  • hāctenus — up to this point, so far

    adverb · also used · classical · Hor. S. 1.4.63: hāctenus haec (Lewis & Short s.v. alius); Traupman 105: up to this point, hāctenus

    Very frequent in Cicero, Lewis & Short notes, to mark where a topic ends: hāctenus haec, so much for that.

  • eō dēcursum est ut (+ subj.) — it came to the point where

    impersonal passive of dēcurrō, with eō, “to that point” · also used · classical · Liv. 26.18: postrēmō eō dēcursum est, ut … (Lewis & Short s.v. dēcurrō); Traupman 105: it got to the point where, eō dēcursum est ut (+ subj.)

Examples

  • Mitte ista, atque ad rem redī.

    Drop all that and get back to the point.Ter. Ad. 2.1.31 (Lewis & Short s.v. redeō)

  • Venī ad rem!

    Get to the point!Traupman 105

  • Tenēsne rem?

    Get the point?Traupman 105

  • Quam ad rem istud rēfert?

    What’s the point of that?Traupman 105

  • Quō ēvādis?

    What’s your point? (What are you driving at?)Traupman 105

  • Quid rētulit tē mittere ad mē litterās?

    What was the point of your writing to me?Traupman 105

  • Hāc dē rē …

    On that point …Traupman 105

  • Nunc cognōsce rem.

    Now here’s the point.Traupman 104

  • hīc; hōc locō

    at this pointTraupman 362

  • Nihil ad rem pertinet.

    You miss the point; that’s beside the point.Traupman 362

See also main, direct, worth.
